AT A GLANCE

hover to pause

🔍
What is it
An econometric & machine-learning study of what predicts how many patents a country files — and which countries file more or fewer than expected.
📊
Data
WIPO/World Bank patent statistics + Our World in Data economics. A 141-country cross-section plus a 2,201-observation panel (136 countries, 2000–2021).
🧩
Methodology
OLS regression, panel fixed effects, a Negative Binomial count model, and Gradient Boosting / Random Forest with country-grouped cross-validation.
💡
Findings
Population & energy use per capita robustly predict patenting. GDP per capita's effect vanishes once fixed effects are added — the income–patents link is mostly between-country, not within-country.

06

Two models, compared

An interpretable linear regression (GDP per capita, population, energy use per capita → log patents) is checked against a Gradient Boosting ensemble on the same three predictors, using 5-fold cross-validation so both scores reflect genuine out-of-sample accuracy.

What the Gradient Boosting model leans on most
The performance gap between the two models is small (ΔR² ≈ 0.05) — a sign the relationship between these fundamentals and patenting activity is close to log-linear.
07

Does it hold up within countries too?

Everything above compares different countries to each other in one year. That leaves an open question: if a single country's GDP per capita rises, does its own patenting rise too — or is the cross-country pattern just "richer countries happen to patent more," for reasons that have nothing to do with income itself? To check, we rebuilt the dataset as a real panel — 2,201 observations, 136 countries, 2000–2021 — and re-ran the regression with country and year fixed effects, which strip out everything constant about a country (legal system, geography, long-run institutions) and ask only what happens when that country's own numbers move.

Coefficient (elasticity) by specification (higher = stronger association with patent filings)
GDP per capita's coefficient falls from 0.51 to 0.02 (statistically indistinguishable from zero) once fixed effects are added — the well-known link between income and patenting looks like a between-country pattern, not evidence that a country patents more as it gets richer. Population and energy use per capita, by contrast, stay positive and significant in every specification, including a Negative Binomial model fit directly on patent counts (the standard approach in the patents-economics literature since Hausman, Hall & Griliches, 1984). Full regression tables and diagnostics are in the accompanying report.

Methodology & sources. Resident patent applications: WIPO Patent Report: Statistics on Worldwide Patent Activity, via World Bank indicator IP.PAT.RESD (1980–2021). Economic data: Our World in Data's country panel (population, GDP, energy use). Regions follow the World Bank's country classification. World map boundaries: Natural Earth via the world-atlas project. Each country's most recent available year was used (median 2021 for patents).

The full methodology, regression tables and equations are in the accompanying working paper: What Drives Global Patenting Activity? (PDF).
